title: Spatial Contaminant Mixtures and Biological Hotspots in a Drinking‐Water Reservoir
content:
ABSTRACT

Reservoirs integrate catchment, tributary, wastewater and shoreline inputs, yet chemical concentrations alone may not capture spatial biological pressure. We evaluated six zones of the Villa Victoria Reservoir, a strategic component of the Cutzamala drinking-water system in central Mexico, during one end-of-rainy-season campaign. Physicochemical variables, five metals, four pesticides, and 14 pharmaceuticals were measured. Common carp (Cyprinus carpio) were exposed for 96 h to site water using three independent replicate aquaria per treatment, with three fish per aquarium; the complete exposure experiment was independently repeated three times. Responses were assessed in blood, gill and liver using oxidative stress biomarkers, micronuclei, histopathology and transcription of eight stress-related genes. Chemical profiles differed among zones associated with municipal drainage, agricultural/livestock activity, tributary inflow, shoreline use and the Cutzamala access area. Aluminium exceeded the PROY-NOM-127-SSA1-2017 contextual comparison value at all sites; dimethoate was highest at agricultural/livestock-associated sites, and metformin was the most abundant pharmaceutical (566.2–3733.6 ng/L). Lipid peroxidation and superoxide dismutase activity increased across all exposure groups, whereas micronucleus frequency increased at Sites 1–5 and was highest at the municipal-drainage site. Tissue lesions and site-specific transcriptional changes provided additional evidence of heterogeneous biological pressure. These results identify biologically responsive zones that were not apparent from conventional physicochemical descriptors alone and support spatially explicit, effect-based monitoring for reservoir management. Because sampling was limited to one campaign, temporal persistence of these patterns requires confirmation.
